correctness.rationale: Equal-coloured leaves agree on atoms and on every diamond formula (false), hence on all terms. Conversely, for a vertex of remaining height d pick a leaf at distance d. With an exact-height test conjoined with the d-fold diamond of this leaf's colour minterm, any matching endpoint is a leaf, is the same leaf by injection, and determines a unique d-th ancestor. At d=h one can omit the exclusion of paths of length h+1, so all singleton formulas have depth at most h, including h=0. A monochromatic path's root and child agree on all formulas through depth h-1 by induction on depth. The count is injections on L labelled leaves times q^(n-L); q=1 works exactly for L=1. The logarithm of the collision product gives the finite positive birthday limit with O(L^3/q^2) error, the upper exponential bound gives the zero limit (including q<L), and the union bound gives the one limit.
residual_risks: The fresh finite computations corroborate the argument only. No assertion about general DAGs with shared descendants, transitive frames or infinite forests was validated.

evidence: Carr covers the abstract equivalences; Agnew's introduction is about local finiteness of transitive K4 algebras; the generic witness paper does not identify leaf-injectivity as sufficient.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Transitive structures are not a broader class containing immediate-child forests. In genuinely broader transition classes (e.g. two roots with a shared child), equal-coloured roots can remain equivalent despite leaf injection. Neither general source supplies the structural reduction, sharp depth or census.

value.rationale: This reduces a whole-frame generation problem to a single leaf-injectivity test regardless of internal labels. It supplies a closed census, exact minimal rank and optimal worst-case formula depth for an entire natural class. The birthday law is a useful consequence, rather than a separate novelty claim.
residual_risks: Optimal depth is uniform worst-case, not asserted to be necessary for each frame or singleton.
